title: Inside a PDF File
plainSentence: A lesson that shows how a PDF file finds its pages, and why deleted content can stay inside it, with editable demos.
pitch: The lesson opens a tiny PDF as plain, line-numbered text on teleprinter-style paper and walks a ladder of five editable demos: object numbers, the cross-reference table of byte offsets, the page tree that sets page order, appended revisions that keep old content, and why a black box is not a delete key. Each rung changes a live file and shows what a reader would do, and two or more self-check questions apply the rules to new files.
firstMinute: A three-line-page PDF is already open in the left pane as text, and the right pane shows the page it draws. Clicking any numbered object lights up its bytes and its entry in the offset table; changing one word of the page text redraws the page and recomputes every offset on screen.
conceptsToLearn: A PDF is a file made of numbered objects that you can read as text.
whyNow: Timeless. Failed black-box redactions and 'deleted' text surviving in files are recurring stories, and almost nobody has seen the structure that explains them.

purposeDetail.concept: How a PDF is organised: numbered objects, a cross-reference table that maps object numbers to byte offsets, a page tree that decides page order, and append-only revisions that explain why 'deleted' or 'blacked out' content can still be in the file.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: People use PDFs daily and trust them to hide things, yet the file layout is rarely shown. Seeing the offsets and the appended revision turns folklore into a mental model.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious non-experts, students, and anyone who redacts or edits documents before sharing them.
misconceptions: Deleting text in a PDF editor removes it from the file.
Drawing a black box over text removes the text.
Pages appear in the order their objects sit in the file.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Pressing 'show revision 1' on a file whose text was 'deleted' brings the old words back from the same bytes, and extracting text under a black box returns it.
demos: Overture: the smallest legal one-page file as numbered lines; click an object to see its bytes
Offsets: edit the text and watch every cross-reference entry recompute; break one on purpose and see the mismatch flagged
Page tree: reorder the Kids list and see the pages swap while the object bytes stay put
Revisions: delete a line, see the appended update with its Prev pointer, then view the file as of revision 1
Black box versus removal: draw a box, extract text, then actually drop the text and compare
checkQuestions: Given a short file listing, what number belongs in the startxref line and why?
Given a Kids list and object order, which page is first?
Given a file with two revisions, is the 'deleted' word still present, and where?
After a black box is drawn over a name, what does text extraction return?

research.summary: Appended revisions, black-box redaction failures and page-tree ordering are all documented outside the standard, and the file-layout facts (startxref, xref entries, trailer Root, Prev chain) are described consistently by independent references, with the free ISO text as the named authority. The lesson can be built from tiny files authored in code, so no third-party documents are bundled.

sources.title: Incremental and Full Save in PDFs (Nutrient)
sources.snippet: Explains that incremental saves append changes with their own cross-reference table and trailer linked by a Prev pointer, so the file keeps a history of earlier content.

sources.title: Didier Stevens blog, May 2008
sources.snippet: A security researcher's note that cutting everything after the first end-of-file marker recovers the original version of an incrementally updated file.
sources.note: Independent confirmation that old revisions remain recoverable.

sources.title: PDF without Adobe 14: PDF is inherently not secure (The Eclectic Light Company)
sources.snippet: Shows that an edited file can still contain the original content, because incremental updating is the common way editors save.
sources.note: Third independent site on surviving content.

sources.title: Why black boxes don't protect sensitive data (Syncfusion)
sources.snippet: Explains that many editors draw a shape over text without changing the content underneath, so the text stays selectable and extractable.
sources.note: Documents the black-box misconception (vendor with an interest, so paired with a second site).

sources.title: The black box in your PDF is a shape, not a delete key (DEV Community)
sources.snippet: A developer article making the same point: a drawn rectangle is an overlay and the underlying text remains in the file.
sources.note: Independent second site for the black-box claim.

sources.title: Understanding PDF Page Trees: Why Page Order Matters (loslab blog)
sources.snippet: Argues page order comes from the Kids array in the page tree, not from object numbers or file position, with a worked example where the last-stored object is the first page.
sources.note: Single-site support for page order; the cited spec section was not checked.

sources.title: The PDF Format (pypdf documentation)
sources.snippet: Library documentation walking through a minimal file: header, objects, xref subsections with 10-digit offsets, trailer with Root and Size, and startxref.
sources.note: Source for the minimal file used as the overture.

sources.title: PDF file format: Basic structure (Infosec Institute)
sources.snippet: A primer stating each xref entry is 20 bytes with the byte offset first, and that readers begin at the end of the file.

sources.title: ISO 32000-1 (PDF 1.7) (PDF Association)
sources.snippet: The PDF Association's page links to Adobe's no-charge copy of ISO 32000-1, identical to the PDF 1.7 reference.
sources.note: Named free authority the lesson links to as reading.

sources.title: Sponsored standards (PDF Association)
sources.snippet: The PDF Association hosts no-cost access to ISO 32000-2 (PDF 2.0), sponsored by member companies.

facts.claim: A PDF incremental update appends new objects, a new cross-reference section and a trailer with a Prev pointer to the end of the file; readers show the newest revision while earlier bytes remain in the file and can be recovered.

Drawing a black rectangle over text in many PDF editors adds a graphic on top and leaves the underlying text in the file, where it can still be selected or extracted; real redaction deletes the content.
Per one publisher's article only, page order comes from the Kids array of the page tree rather than from object numbers or their position in the file; not independently confirmed.

A reader finds the file's structure from the end: startxref gives the byte offset of the last cross-reference section, whose 20-byte entries (10-digit offset, 5-digit generation, n or f) lead to the trailer's Root and the page tree.
ISO 32000-1 (PDF 1.7) is free from Adobe as listed by the PDF Association, and ISO 32000-2 (PDF 2.0) is free through the PDF Association's sponsored-standards page.

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha: the visitor edits a live tiny file at each rung, sees the offsets, order or revision change, and then answers a check question on a new file that applies the rule just shown.
sophisticationHooks: A real in-page parser and writer for tiny files, so every number on screen (offsets, startxref, Prev) is computed, not drawn by hand
Revision viewer that rolls the file back to any appended update
Honest 'what readers do' notes that say behaviour varies between viewers
Self-check questions generated from fresh small files
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: five demos on files authored in code, line-numbered teleprinter-style file view with object highlighting, a minimal page-text renderer for the demo files only, at least four self-check questions, intro and explainer, links to the free standard texts. Cut: arbitrary uploaded files, stream compression, fonts, images.
risks: The page-order claim rests on one site; the lesson must either confirm it against the free ISO text during build or show it as 'per one reference'.
How individual viewers treat a wrong offset varies and was not researched; the page must say 'readers differ' instead of claiming one behaviour.
Redaction is a sensitive topic: the lesson uses made-up sample names only and says it is not legal or security advice.
Overlaps in subject with jester-1 (same file format); if both reach the shortlist only one should win.
